newsitem.title: USA: World Bank, NGOs examine ways to alleviate poverty.
newsitem.headline: World Bank, NGOs examine ways to alleviate poverty.

text.p: An uneasy alliance of the World Bank, governments and community groups wants to help developing countries escape the poverty trap, but both sides admitted on Monday they faced a legacy of mistrust.
The Structural Adjustment Participatory Initiative, formally launched on Monday, follows on from a World Bank promise to tap public opinion about its policies.
It will examine whether demands underpinning current loans are appropriate and help decide what to do next to ensure that World Bank support reaches as many people as possible.
But only seven of the bank's 180 member states have signed up for the initiative. Representatives from non-government organisations (NGOs) admitted they were unsure about working with the bank.

"It is no secret that we from the NGOs and peoples' organisations are quite wary of the bank despite this process," Lidy Nacpil, of the Freedom from Debt Coalition in the Philippines, told the inaugural meeting.
Many of the NGOs have criticised what they describe as a heavy-handed approach from the Washington-based World Bank.

They say structural adjustment policies stressing the need for low inflation and high rates of private ownership have widened the gap between rich and poor and driven people below the poverty line. Women have lost out especially badly.
"Women in the South are the least informed, the least involved and the least capable of coping with adjustment," said Hellen Wangusa, from a Ugandan civil society group.

World Bank President James Wolfensohn said the bank was open to ideas and ready to look at all options, possibly including abandoning some of the tenets of structural reform which have formed the basis of World Bank policy for decades.

"Structural adjustment covers many things," he told the SAPRI meeting. "It was designed to try to develop a macro-economic framework that is positive for all the people in the country and if we learn that some of the things we are doing do not have that affect, I am ready to change it."
He promised to work with the NGOs and listen to them. But he added defensively: "It is not impossible that some of the things we have done over the last 50 years are valid."
Wolfensohn said World Bank rules made clear that the institution could only work with NGOs in a country within the SAPRI initiative if the government was also involved.

The seven founder members of the initiative are Ghana, Mali, Uganda, Zimbabwe, Ecuador, Bangladesh and Hungary. Politicians and NGO representatives from other countries also participated in the SAPRI meeting.

Asked why Mexico had not joined SAPRI, Victor Quintana, a member of Congress for the opposition Party of the Democratic Revolution, said: "The Mexican government does not want an alternative vision to be exposed internationally or even nationally."
Uganda's Secretary of the Treasury, Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile, said his country had signed up for the initiative before the World Bank approached it.

"Structural adjustment has worked in Uganda," he said. "It is true that there are some groups which have not benefited from economic growth, but the answer is to intensify the effort not to abandon it."
